citation: LeadDev (editor Michael Hill), 'The Engineering Leadership Report 2026', 28-page PDF sponsored by Postman. Survey fielded 31 March to 16 April 2026. https://leaddev.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/ENGINEERING_LEADERSHIP_REPORT_2026_FINAL.pdf (URL path indicates June 2026 upload; exact publication date not printed in the extracted text) [uncertain]
source_tier: Company/industry-media research: a vendor-sponsored practitioner survey by a trade publisher. Not peer reviewed.
access_status: Fully read: PDF re-opened and full text extracted with pdftotext -layout (pages 2-28). Charts are text-extracted only, interleaved, so chart values were matched to roles by position and checked against the prose; they were not viewed as images.
sponsor_and_incentive: Sponsored by Postman (page 2, 'A note from Postman'): 'Postman is an API platform for building and using APIs'; it says the results 'reinforce what we hear from the Postman community: as AI accelerates development, teams need more unified, collaborative ways to build, test, and scale.' Postman sells AI-era API tooling, so a narrative of AI-driven pressure on teams suits it. LeadDev sells events and content to engineering leaders. The emotional-drain items sit in a section whose framing is AI as the driver.
exact_quotes: 1) Editor's note (p2): 'Based on responses from 600 engineering leaders, the data tells a story of an industry in genuine transformation under sustained and compounding forces.' 2) Methodology (p28): 'This survey was conducted between 31 March and 16 April 2026. Results are based on the responses of 600 engineers of which 530 completed all the questions that were presented to them. Due to rounding, not all charts add up to 100%.' 3) Key findings (p3): '45% of leaders are working more hours than this time last year.' 4) Hours (p11): 'Just under half (45%) of respondents report working more hours each week than at this point last year, up from 38% in 2025 and 35% in 2024. The biggest increase was among advanced engineers, 53% in 2026 compared to 28% in 2025, followed by managers of engineers (44% vs. 38%) and managers of managers (46% vs. 42%).' 5) Job security (p23): 'Job security concerns have risen for the third consecutive year, with 46% of respondents more worried than at this point last year, up from 42% in 2025 and 39% in 2024. Software engineers are most concerned (61%), followed by tech leads (49%) and managers of engineers (46%).' 6) Interpretation (p23): 'Given that actual layoff rates have not increased significantly, this rising anxiety is almost certainly being driven by AI uncertainty rather than observed job losses.' 7) Burnout (p24): 'Burnout indicators deserve specific attention. CTOs show the most dramatic shift: 54% report feeling emotionally drained from their work at least once a week, compared to just 24% in 2025. This represents a 30-percentage-point increase in a single year.' 8) Chart title (p24): 'At least once a week I feel emotionally drained from my work'. 9) Quote from Thomas Johnson, CTO at Multiplayer (p24): 'CTOs are burning out because AI has given teams virtually infinite capacity, creating relentless pressure to write highly detailed product specs to "feed the beast".' 10) Same speaker (p24-25): 'It is emotionally exhausting to manage an infinitely hungry AI workforce while knowing there is no longer direct human ownership over every line of code.' and leaders 'live in constant fear that a business-killing bug is lingering in some unread, AI-generated corner of the codebase'. 11) Body text (p25): 'The burden of navigating AI transformation at an organizational level, while managing the expectations of boards, investors, and engineering teams simultaneously, appears to be landing particularly heavily on those at the top.' 12) Tech leads (p25): 'Their receipt of regular positive feedback has dropped from 41% to 31%, while cynicism about their jobs is rising.' 13) Motivation free text (p26): 'a babysitting chore, rather than doing interesting work' (respondent describing AI-driven engineering).
date_and_recency: Fielded 31 March to 16 April 2026; PDF hosted under a June 2026 upload path. Annual series with 2024 and 2025 comparisons.
key_claims: AI uncertainty, not layoffs, is driving rising job-security worry (LeadDev's inference; no causal test). CTOs' weekly emotional drain jumped from 24% to 54% year on year. Hours are rising across most roles. Leaders' roles are expanding both technically (37% doing more technical work) and managerially. Tech leads get less positive feedback. Team motivation is down for 41%. One in three managers are considering returning to IC. The report's closing line: 'Working hours are rising. Job security anxieties are growing despite stable layoff rates.'
headline_figures: EMOTIONAL DRAIN ('At least once a week I feel emotionally drained from my work', p24), % agreeing, 2026 vs 2025, read from interleaved chart text and matched by position [uncertain except CTO, which is confirmed in prose]: CTO or equivalent 54% vs 24% (prose-confirmed, +30 points); software engineer 49% vs 39%; advanced engineer 45% vs 46%; tech lead 39% vs 46%; manager of engineers 48% vs 49%; manager of managers 46% vs 56%. Chart values for non-CTO roles are not stated in prose, and the assignment of the two numbers per role to years is inferred from CTO ordering (2026 first, 2025 second). So only the CTO jump is a clear year-on-year rise; most other roles are flat or lower, and the manager-of-managers figure appears to fall 10 points. OTHER ITEMS, 2026 vs 2025 where read: work demands interfere with personal life at least weekly: software engineer 37/32, advanced engineer 39/31, tech lead 31/31, manager of engineers 41/36, manager of managers 30/37, CTO 51/51 and 48 (chart text shows 51, 51, 48; ordering unclear) [uncertain]. Positive feedback weekly: tech lead 31% in 2026 vs 41% in 2025 (prose); CTO 26/28; manager of managers 16/19; manager of engineers 24/22. Cynical about job weekly: CTO 38% vs 22% (chart, ordering inferred) [uncertain]. HOURS ('Are you working more or less hours each week than this time last year?', p11), % more hours, 2026 vs 2025: all respondents 45% vs 38% (35% in 2024); software engineer 35/31; advanced engineer 53/28; tech lead 44/48; manager of engineers 44/38; manager of managers 46/42; CTO 46/52 (CTO more-hours share FELL, 52% to 46%, per chart text). JOB SECURITY (more concerned than a year ago, p23): all 46% (42% in 2025, 39% in 2024); software engineer 61 (vs 41); advanced engineer 45 (vs 37); tech lead 49 (vs 61); manager of engineers 46 (vs 44); manager of managers 45 (vs 37); CTO 43 (vs 28). Team less motivated than 12 months ago: 41% (44% in 2025). More technical work: 37% (25% in 2025). Considering moving from management to IC: 'one in three' managers (24% in 2025 for the comparison per chart text).
sample_unit_and_population: Method: 600 respondents, 530 completed all questions presented to them. Methodology page calls them 'engineers' while the editor's note and headline say 'engineering leaders'; the sample includes software engineers (9%), tech leads (11%), senior individual contributors (16%), managers of engineers (37%), managers of managers (18%), CTO or equivalent (6%), other (3%), so many respondents are not leaders. Role shares are read from a pie chart in the methodology; implied approximate base sizes from 600 total (my arithmetic, assuming percentages apply to all 600, not the 530 completers): software engineer ~54, tech lead ~66, senior IC/advanced engineer ~96, manager of engineers ~222, manager of managers ~108, CTO or equivalent ~36, other ~18 [uncertain]. The report prints NO per-role base sizes and no margin of error. The CTO subgroup of roughly 36 means one respondent is about 3 percentage points, and the 24% to 54% shift rests on a very small, possibly non-matched subgroup. Location: USA 32%, Europe excl. UK and Germany 23%, UK 20%, Germany 9%, Asia 5%, Canada 4%, Mexico/Central/South America 4%, Oceania 3%, Africa 1%, Other 3% (approximate chart reads). Recruitment channel and sampling method are not stated (LeadDev audience is likely; not confirmed) [uncertain]. 2025 and 2024 comparison samples and their sizes are not given, and it is not stated that they are the same people. Software engineers: yes, all respondents are in software engineering roles.
observed_vs_stated: Entirely self-reported survey answers (single-item agreement with 'at least once a week I feel emotionally drained'). No behavioural or physiological data. Causes are the editor's and interviewees' interpretation.
what_it_measures_or_defines: Burnout is not defined or measured with a validated instrument. The proxy is one self-report item, 'At least once a week I feel emotionally drained from my work', plus sibling items (cynical about job weekly, work interferes with personal life weekly, positive feedback weekly). The report uses the phrase 'burnout indicators' and 'burning out' loosely. The item is similar in spirit to emotional exhaustion items in burnout inventories but is a single item with a weekly-frequency cutoff, and the report cites no instrument [uncertain whether adapted from a published scale].
mechanism_or_cause: Attributed to AI: leaders face 'relentless pressure to write highly detailed product specs to feed the beast' (Johnson, CTO at Multiplayer), managing an 'infinitely hungry AI workforce' without direct human ownership of every line of code, fear of an unread AI-generated bug, and managing expectations of boards, investors and teams. Job-security worry is put down to 'AI uncertainty' and 'loss of clarity' (quote attributed to Rao; role not recorded here). Motivation falls because 'rewarding creative work' is displaced by 'maintenance and review of AI-generated code'. These are interpretations from interviews and free text, not tested causes.
interventions_and_effects: None tested. The report ends with a general call for 'the trust, the clarity, the investment in people' and leadership that holds AI ambitions 'alongside its human responsibilities'. No effect sizes.
transfer_to_software_teams: Directly about software engineering roles, so no domain gap. But it is a mixed sample dominated by managers, with a tiny CTO subgroup, and it speaks to senior leaders' feelings about AI, not to engineers doing agent oversight day to day. It does not isolate oversight or review of agent output; the nearest hint is the 'unread, AI-generated corner of the codebase' quote and the 'babysitting chore' free-text.
limitations_stated: Only the methodology note: 'Due to rounding, not all charts add up to 100%.' and the 530 of 600 completion figure. No stated discussion of sampling, self-selection, weighting, margin of error, role bases or non-response. No limitations section.
counter_evidence: Within the report's own chart text: emotional drain is flat or lower in 2026 versus 2025 for advanced engineers, tech leads and managers of engineers, and appears lower for managers of managers, so the CTO spike is not a leader-wide trend [uncertain for non-CTO ordering]. Share of CTOs working more hours fell from 52% to 46%. Job-security concern for tech leads fell from 61% to 49%. Software engineers (non-leaders) report the highest job-security worry (61%) and a weekly drain level (49%, chart read, uncertain) close to the CTO figure (54%). Fielded in a different cohort each year (not stated otherwise), so year-on-year changes in small subgroups may be sampling noise. No source in this file tests the AI-causation claim; layoffs being stable and anxiety being AI-driven is the report's inference. Check other files in this research folder for burnout instruments and base rates.

usable_claim: In LeadDev's 2026 survey of 600 people in engineering roles (fielded 31 March to 16 April, sponsored by Postman), 54% of CTOs or equivalents said they felt emotionally drained from their work at least once a week, up from 24% in 2025. Overall, 45% said they were working more hours than a year earlier. The CTO group is small (roughly 6% of the sample, on the order of three dozen people), the measure is one self-report question, and the report's AI explanation comes from interviews, not testing. Safe to cite as a signal of what some senior leaders say, not as a measured burnout rate.
do_not_use: Do not call it burnout prevalence or say 54% of CTOs are burned out. Do not describe it as a survey of 'leaders' only (the methodology says engineers and the sample includes ICs). Do not generalise the CTO jump to all engineers or managers (other roles are flat or lower, chart reads uncertain). Do not state causation by AI. Do not quote per-role base sizes as reported (they are my estimates). Do not use the non-CTO chart numbers without checking the chart image. Do not present Johnson's quote as a finding.
